g.text: Segments, a sparse index, and zero-copy - and each one dictates an API decision
The most consequential is zero-copy: it only works if the bytes on disk are byte-identical to the bytes on the wire.
A partition is a sequence of segment files, named for their base offset
sealed - immutable, safe to read lock-free
.index
.timeindex
sealed - immutable
.index
.timeindex
ACTIVE - appends land here
.index
.timeindex
Retention becomes unlink() - an O(1) syscall reclaiming a gigabyte. One giant file would mean copying the surviving tail
forward to release the head. That alone justifies segmenting; finding an offset then becomes a binary search over filenames.
The index is SPARSE - one entry every ~4 KB, not per message
.index (offset -> byte position)
Lookup: binary search for the largest entry <= target, then SCAN FORWARD
inside a 4 KB window. One index lookup plus one short sequential read.
A 1 GB segment of 1 KB messages holds ~1 million messages. Indexing every
one costs ~8 MB of index per GB and turns index lookups into their own
random-read problem. Sparse costs ~16 KB/GB - small enough to mmap and
effectively always resident.
The principle worth extracting
A sparse index trades a BOUNDED SEQUENTIAL SCAN for a large reduction in index size. Sequential
scanning is nearly free here (244x), so spending a 4 KB scan to save 500x on index size is obviously
right. In a random-access system the same trade would be wrong. Index density is a function of how
cheap your scan is.
Batching is the primary dial - and it does THREE jobs at once
amortizes syscall + network
488k syscalls/sec -> ~31k.
A 16-message batch is one round trip.
makes writes truly sequential
16 KB lands as one contiguous extent;
1 KB writes interleave and fragment.
enables cross-message compression
shared dictionary: 5-10x as a batch
versus ~2x individually.
The third is easy to miss and often the biggest: the batch is stored AND replicated compressed, so batching cuts disk usage,
replication bandwidth and consumer fetch bandwidth simultaneously. A 500 MB/sec ingest at 5x is 100 MB/sec of real disk traffic.
linger_ms = 0 -> lowest latency, smallest batches, lowest throughput
linger_ms = 100 -> highest throughput, +100ms at p99
This is exactly how the 'configurable latency versus throughput' requirement is met:
the same code serves a 5ms order pipeline and a 500 MB/sec log aggregator by changing
one number. And it is why a routing tier was rejected - a middle tier never sees one
producer's messages for one partition together, so it cannot batch them at all.
Zero-copy, and the API decision it forces
disk -> page cache -> APPLICATION BUFFER -> socket buffer -> NIC
2 extra copies + 2 context switches, pure waste
disk -> page cache -> NIC
sendfile() / splice()
The architectural consequence matters more than the performance one: the broker CANNOT decompress, re-frame or transform a
message - the moment it touches the payload it must copy into user space and the optimization is gone. So the message format
is IDENTICAL for producer, broker storage and consumer; compression is end-to-end; and the broker is deliberately ignorant of
message contents. That is why broker-side filtering is awkward and why poison-message policy has to live in the consumer.
